Sesquicentennial Celebration
The New York Sesquicentennial Celebration dinner on
November 18 provided an ideal opportunity for making new
friends and renevsdng old acquaintances, as well as singing vrith
fervor the old Psi U favorites.
Psi U's from far and wide have been gathering in enthusiastic
groups to celebrate the Fraternity's 150th Anniversary. Special
Sesquicentennial Celebration dinners in honor of this momen
tous occasion have been held in six cities thus far, with many
more planned for the spring.
Each has included toasts to the President ofthe United States
and the Queen ofthe British Commonwealth by noteworthy Psi
Upsilon representatives. In addition, special keepsake banquet
programs have been used and the very handsome Sesquicenten
nial commemorative plate has been available for purchase.
The following are some of the highlights of these dinners:
Buffalo
This special series of banquets was inaugurated by the
Niagara Frontier Alumni Association of Psi Upsilon on Novem
ber 17, 1983, at the Saturn Club in Buffalo. Unique among the
Fraternity's alumni groups because of its blend of membership
from both the United States and Canada, the Association hosted
a spirited Sesquicentennial Celebration dinner, presided over
by Sewell F. Hubbard, Epsilon Phi '38. Arrangements were
completed by W. Barry Mallon, Gamma '44.
New York
Held at the New York University Club on November 18,
1983, this dinner was attended by 119 representatives from 23
different Chapters. The program was highlighted by the con
veying of the Distinguished Alumnus Award to Thomas H.
Wyman, Gamma '51. Brother Wyman, who is Chairman ofthe
Board, President, and Chief Executive Officer of CBS, Inc.,
graciously accepted the newly created award and spoke elo
quently about his Psi U experience.
Also honored were past presidents ofthe Executive Council:
Jerome W. Brush, Jr. ,
Delta Delta '39; Robert W. Morey, Pi
'20; and Robert W. Parsons, Xi '22. Brother Morey was on hand
to accept his citation. He delivered a stirring address, as only
one can do who speaks from the heart, on the intrinsic value of
Psi Upsilon. Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, served as the able
master of ceremonies, and David C. Weld, Zeta '46, extended
his greetings on behalf of the New York Metropolitan Associa
tion, which hosted the occasion.
Robert A. Burch, Upsilon '55, delivered the invocation, and
appropriate toasts were made by General Frank L. Howley,
Delta '25, and David A. B. Brovm, Epsflon Phi '66. J. Russefl
McShane, Delta '32, President ofthe Executive Council, spoke
on behalf of the Fraternity's administrative body.
Atlanta

took place on December 10, 1983 when the Fraternity's third
Sesquicentennial Celebration dinner was hosted by the Psi
Upsilon Society of Georgia. Stephen L. King, Gamma Tau '75,
served as Dinner Chairman for the occasion, which included
spouses and dates. The festivities were highhghted by the
address of Wifliam R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66, Secretary of

as master of ceremonies, and the invocation was delivered by

This is the seventh in a continuing series
of articles profiling the members of the
Executive Council.
As a charter member of the Nu Alpha
Chapter, Class of 1971, and its president
from 1970 to 1971, Charles M. Hafl
formed an involvement with Psi Upsilon
that has only intensified through the
years, despite the eventual demise ofhis
Chapter just four years after its installa
tion.
Chuck Hall became a member of the
Executive Councfl in 1974 and has served
as Chairman of the Finance Committee
since June, 1982. In the latter capacity,
he has assumed the awesome responsibil
ity ofoverseeing the Fraternity's financial
operations. Under his leadership, Psi U
was able to submit to the last Convention
a balanced budget for 1983-84, thus re
versing the recent trend of operating at a
deficit.
But Chuck Hafl's commitment to Psi
Upsilon has not been limited to his Ex
ecutive Council participation. As a resi
dent ofAtlanta, Georgia, he has taken the
nearby Gamma Tau Chapter at the Geor
gia Institute of Technology under his
wing. He served as president of the Psi
Upsilon Society of Georgia from 1978 to
1982 and as treasurer since then.
It was Chuck Hall who negotiated the
purchase of a house for the Gamma Tau
Chapter in 1978 and who has dealt with
the zoning board through the years to
modify restrictions so that a fraternity
house could operate in a mainly residen
tial area. Brother Hall is presently in
volved in laying the groundwork for the
acquisition of a new, larger house to bet
ter meet the needs of the expanding
Gamma Tau Chapter.
Chuck Hall's business career has been
no less impressive than his accomplish
ments within Psi U. After graduating
from Washington and Lee as a Dean's
List student with a B.A. degree in poli
ties, he entered the U. S. Army Reserve
as a 2nd lieutenant, on active duty from
1971 to 1972, and eventually received an
honorable discharge as a captain. He pro
ceeded to the Emory University Lamar
School of Law, where he again received
Dean's List honors and was rated in the
top 15% ofhis class.

Undergraduate Leaders Meet in Paoli
Some skeptical Psi U brethren thought
that it was a bad omen to start the first
meeting of the newly-formed Under
graduate Advisory Board on Friday the
13th, but, thankfully, they were proved
wrong. The eight undergraduate leaders
who gathered at the Fraternity office on
January 13-15 wifl attest to the meeting's
success.
Created at the Sesquicentennial Con
vention last August for the purpose of
increasing undergraduate knowledge of
and participation in Fraternity govern
ance, the Undergraduate Advisory Board
is comprised ofthe nine Regional Repre
sentatives elected at the Convention. It
was stipulated that they meet at least
once each year to discuss in detail the
pertinent issues facing the Fraternity and
to formulate concrete suggestions and/or
recommendations to be brought before
the Executive Council.
After a pleasant opening luncheon on
Friday, the professional staff members
concentrated on briefing the undergradu
ates on the role of the Executive Council
and of the Regional Representatives, on
Psi U's pohcies and philosophies, and on
recent Executive Councfl decisions. The
UAB members received a Class A tour of
the ofBce and archives by tour guide Hen
ry B. Poor, Gamma '39, Executive Vice
President. They also had an opportunity
to meet the entire staff, each of whom
described in detail his/her individual
duties and responsibiliries within the
overall framework.
By Saturday morning the group was
ready to get down to some heavy duty
discussion on the issues. Topics included
the role of the UAB in light of the pro
posed Executive Councfl realignment;
evaluation ofthe Field Director program
and suggestions for improvement; the
advantages and disadvantages of produc
ing officer manuals, pledge manuals, etc.
and recommendations for their content;
the effectiveness of Psi Upsilon's recently
legislated hazing policy and the related
importance of a constructive pledge
education program; the Fraternity's phi
losophy of relative autonomy and how it
can adversely affect inter-chapter rela
tions if not understood properly; the con
tinuation or appearance of certain dis
criminatory practices within some Chap
ters and methods to eliminate them;
means to educate undergraduates on the
use and abuse of alcohol and drugs, in
cluding the endorsement of strict antitralRcking legislation; and the direction
the Fraternity should take in its reactiva
tion and expansion efforts.
Lengthy discussions also ensued on
ways to combat specific problems being
experienced by some of our Chapters,
such as financial difficulties, internal fric
tion, poor rush, weak alumni relations,
etc. The sharing of ideas by members of
Chapters whose operations often vary
widely produced some concrete and di
verse suggestions for addressing specific
difficulties and improving overall opera
tions.
Lest one worry that the weekend was
not balanced with a little recreational
activity, it should be mentioned that
Henry and Mary Poor hosted a delightful
dinner party at their home on Friday
evening. The Field Directors' apartment
served as "home" for the visitors, and it
was there that the most social interaction
took place. The relaxed, informal atmos
phere provided the perfect setting for
sharing ideas and exchanging information
and, as a result, of getting to know and
trust one another. The open and straight
forward discussions which transpired,
often on very controversial subjects, were
a clear indication of the mutual respect
that was shared by all.

members were in attendance at the UAB
meeting in Paoli: MarkD. Bauer, Omega
'83, Field Director; James C. Bockelman,
Pi '85; James H. Bresson, Psi '83, Field
Director; Victor T. Gainor, 111, Delta '83;
Alan N. Greenspan, Gamma '84; James

Jr., Kappa '85; Kathleen M. McGlone,
